findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever content the mutable URL returns. A compromised origin, DNS/proxy path, or changed installer can run arbitrary commands in the build environment and silently alter the produced image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The image build downloads and executes whatever bytes are currently served by a mutable HTTPS URL. A compromised origin, DNS/TLS trust failure, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code during the build and alter the produced image.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Without pipefail or an explicit download-and-check step, a failed curl can provide empty input to sh; sh exits successfully for empty input, so Docker can produce an image without the intended installation.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded install script
findings.whyItBreaks: Each build fetches mutable content from a remote URL and pipes it directly to sh. If the endpoint, DNS route, or upstream artifact is compromised or changes, arbitrary code runs during the image build.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key at src/store.go:10, but this exported function discards that error and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose legitimate value is empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for absent keys, but this exported wrapper discards it and returns "", indistinguishable from a present key whose value is legitimately empty. Callers cannot safely distinguish lookup failure from valid data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in public loader
findings.whyItBreaks: Ignoring Load's ErrMissing makes an absent key return "", identical to a key explicitly stored with an empty value. As an exported API, every caller is forced to treat lookup failure as real data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every job result was sent. It now launches sends asynchronously and immediately returns, so a caller can treat return as completion and close results, causing a goroutine to panic on send; callers can also observe incomplete or reordered results.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every result had been sent. The new goroutines let it return immediately; a caller that closes results after Run returns will cause pending goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel". Callers also cannot rely on all results being available when Run completes.

findings.title: Preserve completion before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send now runs after Run may return. A caller that invokes Run, then closes results to signal completion can race with these goroutines and panic with "send on closed channel"; callers that consume immediately after Run also no longer have a completion guarantee.

findings.title: Require both admin role and tenant ownership for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes any administrator to delete records in other tenants, and authorizes any non-admin user to delete any record in their own tenant. The previous predicate required both safeguards.

findings.title: Require admin and matching tenant before deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || returns true for a non-admin in the record's tenant and for an admin from a different tenant. The prior predicate required both conditions, so this changes a delete authorization boundary and enables unauthorized or cross-tenant record deletion.

findings.title: Require tenant-matched administrators to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `||` makes `canDeleteRecord` return true for any same-tenant session even when `isAdmin` is false, and for any administrator even when the record belongs to another tenant. Both cases were denied before, so this removes the role requirement and tenant isolation from a destructive authorization decision.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings errors before saving
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid JSON or malformed settings previously caused updateFontSize to stop before calling save. The new catch returns defaults instead, so updateFontSize sets the requested font size and persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}, silently replacing the user's malformed/corrupted settings and hiding the parse failure.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid saved settings now produce the same Settings value as valid default settings. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and calls save, overwriting the corrupt original with {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}; previously the parse error propagated and prevented the write.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-settings errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid JSON or invalid settings fields now return a legitimate Settings value instead of throwing. updateFontSize therefore saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":size} over malformed stored settings, whereas it previously propagated the error and performed no save. Exported callers also cannot distinguish parse failure from an actual default-valued configuration.

findings.title: Use the requested branch commit for artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: The report's builtFrom field remains build.ref(branch), but artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). When the requested branch and verified ref differ, the report combines the branch commit with another commit's artifacts.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For a branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom is set to build.ref(branch) but artifacts are fetched with build.ref("verified"). The resulting report falsely associates verified artifacts with the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Keep artifacts tied to the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The report declares builtFrom as build.ref(branch), but artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). For any requested branch whose ref differs from verified, the report combines the branch commit with another commit's artifacts.

findings.title: Restore the limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For limit=20, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most 20. renderFeed then writes every returned entry into its nominally 20-slot output array, extending it beyond 20 entries.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed calls it with 20, so feeds with more than 20 entries now return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all entries rather than at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, so an input with more than 20 entries now produces a feed longer than 20.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: For any stale entry, the body now omits its row while the unchanged header still receives entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry claims '# entry-count: 2' but contains one entry row, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering removes stale entries from the body, but the unchanged header still uses entries.length. A manifest with one live and one stale entry declares "# entry-count: 2" while containing one row, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Keep entry-count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: For entries containing one live and one stale item, this filter emits one data row while the unchanged header call still declares `# entry-count: 2`. Consumers relying on the manifest's count can reject or misprocess the manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported FormatLegacyID symbol is a source-incompatible API change: any downstream package calling it will fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore the removed public legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported Go API. Removing it is a source-incompatible change: any downstream module using ids.FormatLegacyID will fail to compile when upgrading, with no replacement or deprecation path in this diff.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote public export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function in the base revision but is no longer exported. Any consumer importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module and is removed rather than retained as a compatibility wrapper. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, while the new quoteShipping export is in a different module and does not preserve that import path.

findings.title: Reject malformed stored hashes instead of raising
findings.whyItBreaks: token_hash() returns an ASCII string, but hmac.compare_digest() raises TypeError when stored_hash is a non-ASCII string (for example a corrupted persisted value "é"). Previously equality returned false, so guard() returned 401; now the exception escapes guard() and turns an invalid credential into a server error.

findings.title: Restore execute’s string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws before producing a value. Consumers can no longer transform input or rely on the function’s declared result.

findings.title: Restore execute's declared string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws "always fails". This makes the public API unusable and regresses the prior uppercase transformation.

findings.title: Restore execute's result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute function now fails, including valid string inputs that previously returned their uppercase form.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: Active viewers previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only" at line 25. The new rejection returns "rejected" at line 24 first, so the viewer-specific behavior is now unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve viewer access to the read-only handler path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only". This new rejection returns "rejected" first, so handle's explicit viewer behavior at line 25 can never run.

findings.title: Keep viewer requests eligible for the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now returns "rejected" at handle() before reaching its dedicated "read-only" branch. Before this change, the same request returned "read-only".

findings.title: Do not require payment before saving drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: An order with state="draft" and payment="missing" previously passed canProceed and saveDraft returned "saved". The added payment condition makes saveDraft return "blocked", although saving a draft is independent of payment.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: The new payment condition makes canProceed({ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }) false. saveDraft uses this shared predicate, so an unpaid draft now returns "blocked" instead of "saved"; payment may govern submission but does not govern persisting a draft.

findings.title: Keep draft saving independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: For an order `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, the new payment condition makes `canProceed` false. `saveDraft` therefore returns "blocked", even though saving a draft must remain possible before payment.

findings.title: Read files from the selected commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot advertises that channel’s commit but contains stable’s file list. Consumers will publish or inspect content that does not correspond to snapshot.commit or snapshot.channel.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the returned channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies the channel head while Snapshot.files describes stable. Consumers restoring, comparing, or publishing this snapshot receive an internally inconsistent snapshot; publishing also now requires a stable ref even when the requested channel exists.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned commit identifies the requested channel but files are loaded from stable. Consumers receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect the wrong revision.

findings.title: Honor the supplied limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling `build("x", limit=1)` still returns 10 entries because the loop is controlled by the unchanged constant `max_count = 10`. The added public parameter promises callers they can cap the returned data, but the implementation silently ignores it.

findings.title: Honor the supplied limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=2)` still iterates `range(max_count)` where `max_count` is hard-coded to 10, so callers cannot obtain the requested capped result despite the public parameter contract.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises callers control over the result bound, but the body always sets `max_count = 10`; e.g. `build("x", 2)` still returns ten items.

findings.title: Validate positivity before returning the parsed integer
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1 and parse_positive_int('0') returns 0, despite the exported name promising a positive result. Callers can therefore receive or charge negative/zero amounts while relying on the new contract.

findings.title: Validate that parsed amounts are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` accepts `0` and negative integers because it only calls `int()`. `charge` consumes this result at line 6, so `charge(-1)` returns `-100` despite the parser's positive-value contract.

findings.title: Preserve the read_int public API
findings.whyItBreaks: Renaming the public module function removes read_int, so existing consumers upgrading this module receive AttributeError or ImportError instead of the prior conversion behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation copied df and applied updates to that copy. The changed code writes through df.loc and returns the same object, so callers that retain df will observe their original data unexpectedly altered.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying mappings. This change writes into the passed DataFrame, so callers that retain df as an original/snapshot will have it unexpectedly overwritten when they use the returned transformed value.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before applying mappings. This now writes through to the caller-provided DataFrame, so callers that retain and reuse the input see values unexpectedly changed.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, contradicting its public name and allowing `charge("-1")` to return `-100` instead of rejecting or neutralizing a non-positive amount.

findings.title: Make parse_positive_int reject non-positive input
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public API promises a positive integer, but its body accepts every parseable i64. For example, parse_positive_int("-1") returns -1, and charge("-1") consequently returns -100 instead of rejecting an invalid amount.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-value contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns -1 because `str::parse` accepts signed integers. Its caller then produces a negative charge (-100), contradicting the new public contract that callers may rely on for validation.

findings.title: Borrow items in debug output
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` uses a moved value, causing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Borrow `items` in the debug statement
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` then borrows a moved value and Rust emits E0382.

findings.title: Avoid moving `items` in the debug statement
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns the owned Vec; the semicolon drops that returned value, leaving `items` moved before `items.len()` on line 3. Rust reports use of moved value and the crate cannot compile.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than "latest", fromRevision still advertises the pinned revision but changedPaths is computed from latest. Consumers replaying the changeset on fromRevision will omit all changes between the pinned revision and latest (and may receive an empty set when latest is the current revision).

findings.title: Compute paths from the revision exposed by the changeset
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to a revision different from `latest`, `fromRevision` remains the pinned revision while `changedPaths` is computed from `latest`. Consumers replaying these paths on `fromRevision` receive paths for the wrong base, causing omitted or incorrect changes.

findings.title: Compute paths from the returned base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than latest, changedPaths is computed from latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. Consumers replaying those paths on fromRevision, as the exported Changeset contract requires, receive a changeset for the wrong base and can omit or apply incorrect changes.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any deployment that applies 0002 will fail that query with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`. Any path using that query after upgrade fails with a missing-column SQL error.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users, causing a no-such-column SQL error on upgraded databases.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential loading
findings.whyItBreaks: The committed bk_live_ credential is exposed to every repository reader and will be used by every deployment regardless of its configured BILLING_API_KEY. The key cannot be rotated or scoped per environment without a source change, and exposure requires revocation.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential loading
findings.whyItBreaks: The committed bk_live_ credential is exposed to every repository reader and is used regardless of BILLING_API_KEY. Rotation or revocation now requires a code release, and deployments configured with their own billing credentials will silently charge against the shared live account instead.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: This embeds a `bk_live_` credential in source and returns it for every environment. The secret is now exposed to anyone with repository access, cannot follow environment-specific configuration or normal secret rotation, and callers succeed with production credentials even when BILLING_API_KEY is intentionally unset.

findings.title: Restore admin-only purge authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: An admin now returns "forbidden" before deletion, while any non-admin with an archived project passes both guards and invokes db.delete(project.id). This reverses the prior admin-only protection on a destructive operation.

findings.title: Require an admin before purging a project
findings.whyItBreaks: The new early return forbids admins, then permits any non-admin to reach db.delete for an archived project. Previously only an admin could purge an archived project, so this is an authorization bypass and data-loss path.

findings.title: Require admins before purging archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: For an archived project, user.isAdmin=false now bypasses both forbidden returns and calls db.delete at line 14, while an admin is denied. The prior implementation permitted only admin users to purge archived projects, so this is an authorization bypass with irreversible deletion.

findings.title: Preserve fallback settings for missing config files
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when the requested path does not exist (line 7). Removing the None fallback makes startup evaluate settings["workers"] on None, raising TypeError; before this change the same path started with one worker.

findings.title: Preserve startup behavior when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings` returns `None` for a nonexistent path at app/config.py:6-7. Previously `startup` converted that case to the default worker configuration; now `settings["workers"]` raises `TypeError`, so a startup invocation without a settings file fails instead of using one worker.

findings.title: Preserve default settings when the config file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path, and startup now immediately indexes that None value. Previously this path used one worker and the default region; it now raises TypeError before startup can proceed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil. Callers of this exported function therefore cannot distinguish a failed payment from a successful one and may fulfill an unpaid order.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error but returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a completed one and may persist or report it as successful.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. Callers cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a successful one and may continue fulfillment or record payment as complete.

findings.title: Preserve tenant identity in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches setting `name`, `settingsFor` stores it as `settings:name`. A subsequent request for the same name from tenant B hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`, despite the store contract being tenant-scoped.

score.error: malformed critic output: finding was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping to the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads `name`, its fetched value is stored under `settings:${name}`. A subsequent read for tenant B with the same name hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`, leaking tenant-scoped configuration across tenants.

findings.title: Preserve construction without requiring a new Store argument
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory was previously constructible with `new Inventory()`. The new required constructor parameter makes every existing TypeScript consumer fail to compile until it supplies a Store, despite no migration path or default implementation.

findings.title: Avoid changing reserve from a boolean to a Promise
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers of the exported synchronous `reserve()` API receive a Promise instead of a boolean. JavaScript callers such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` now take the success branch even when stock is empty because Promise objects are truthy; TypeScript callers expecting a boolean also stop typechecking.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields before stock is decremented. Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls with stock=1 both read 1, both save 0, and both return true, granting two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either await completes. Both save 0, both return true, and two units are reserved although only one was available.

findings.title: Preserve zero-argument Inventory construction
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported and previously had an implicit zero-argument constructor. Existing TypeScript consumers using new Inventory() now fail to compile, while JavaScript consumers create an instance whose later successful reserve call throws when accessing this.store.save.

findings.title: Avoid changing reserve from synchronous to asynchronous
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers expecting a boolean no longer type-check. Existing JavaScript conditionals such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` now test a truthy Promise, so they take the success branch even when stock is empty.

findings.title: Migrate retry to the new millisecond backoff unit
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still passes `backoff(a) * 1000` to `setTimeout`. The first failed retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1,000 ms; capped retries wait over eight hours.

findings.title: Update retry to stop multiplying millisecond backoff
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff now returns milliseconds (1,000–30,000), but retry still multiplies its result by 1,000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. A first failed attempt waits 1,000 seconds instead of 1 second, and capped retries wait over 8 hours instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Remove the extra retry millisecond conversion
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). The first failed attempt therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16m 40s) instead of 1 second; higher attempts wait up to 30,000,000 ms (about 8h 20m).

findings.title: Propagate the final file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. Previously, after a successful writer flush, Save returned f.Close() so callers could detect a final writeback failure; it now returns nil. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat an unsuccessfully finalized file as successfully saved.

findings.title: Propagate file close failures
findings.whyItBreaks: After a successful flush, the deferred f.Close() error is ignored, so Save can return nil even when final file completion reports an error. The previous implementation returned that error to the caller.

findings.title: Propagate the close failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When Flush succeeds, Save evaluates and returns nil before the deferred Close runs. The deferred call's error is discarded, so a close failure is reported as a successful save; previously Save returned that error.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is already an exclusive bound, but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes the row at `end - 1`. Thus a page of size 10 returns 9 rows, and a one-row final page returns no rows; `render_page` and `summarize` consequently drop data.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The documented half-open bounds end at the first index after the page, but range(start, end - 1) stops two indices before that boundary. Thus a full page of three rows returns only two rows, and a one-row page returns no rows. render_page and summarize consequently omit the last row of every rendered page.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: `_window_bounds` defines `end` as exclusive, but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes the last valid index. A one-row page becomes empty, and every full or partial page drops its final row; `summarize` therefore omits rows from its output.

findings.title: Return entries only while their TTL is valid
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so for a positive TTL this condition is false and get() deletes it. Once its TTL has expired, the condition becomes true and get() returns stale data indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second done job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return entries while they are still within the TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails the `> ttlMs` check, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs without index skipping
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward `forEach` shifts the next job into the removed index, then `forEach` advances past it. Two adjacent completed jobs therefore leave one completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired cache-entry condition
findings.whyItBreaks: Fresh entries (age <= ttlMs) are now deleted and returned as null, while entries older than ttlMs are returned. This reverses the cache's expiration behavior and can serve stale values indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue. This also changes the prior public behavior by mutating the caller's array.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator compares numbers as strings. For scores [2, 10, 9] and n=2, rankScores returns [9, 2, 10], making the cutoff 2; topPlayers then returns the first two input players [2, 10] instead of the two highest-scoring players [10, 9].

findings.title: Sort numeric scores with a comparator
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [3, 100, 20] and n=1, rankScores returns [3, 20, 100], so topPlayers uses 3 as the cutoff and returns the first input player rather than the 100-score player.

findings.title: Restore numeric ordering before computing the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts values as strings. For players ordered as score 90 then 100 with n=1, rankScores returns [90, 100], making the cutoff 90; filtering then slicing preserves input order and returns the 90-score player instead of the 100-score player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Normal string equality can return after the first differing character, making verification time depend on the length of the correct signature prefix. A remote caller can use repeated requests to infer the expected HMAC incrementally and eventually submit a forged signature that reaches processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can return after the first mismatching character, exposing comparison timing for attacker-controlled signatures. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` was specifically designed to avoid this leakage; a remote attacker can use repeated requests to incrementally infer the expected HMAC and bypass the authentication check in `handle`.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can return earlier for a mismatching prefix, allowing an attacker able to repeatedly submit signatures and measure responses to infer the expected HMAC one character at a time. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` avoids this timing side channel.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Exiting the transaction at line 23 commits the ledger insert before either balance update runs. If either subsequent UPDATE fails, the transfer returns an error with a committed ledger record and partially applied or unapplied balances; previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits, then the debit and credit execute outside that atomic boundary. If either balance update fails, the committed ledger entry remains; if the second update fails, the source is debited without crediting the destination.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after recording the ledger entry. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while balances are unchanged or only the source account is debited. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation deliberately derived all three components with UTC getters. The new local-time getters produce a different billing key for the same instant on hosts outside UTC; for example, an instant at 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in an Americas timezone. This also changes sameBillingDay results based on server timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the prior UTC calculation with the process host's local timezone. For example, with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, Date("2025-01-01T00:30:00Z") now returns "2024-12-31" instead of the prior "2025-01-01", so the same instant can be assigned to different billing days depending on deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The same instant is now assigned to different billing days depending on the runtime timezone. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 on a UTC-8 host, whereas the prior implementation consistently returned 2026-01-01.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a profile for tenant A/account X is cached, a read for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. This breaks tenant isolation and can expose the wrong tenant's profile data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After reading tenant A/account X, a later read for tenant B/account X uses the same `account` key and returns tenant A's cached Profile at line 16 without calling `fetchProfile` for tenant B.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a profile for tenant A/account X is cached, a request for tenant B/account X returns that cached Profile at lines 15-16 without calling fetchProfile. This exposes the first tenant's profile to another tenant and returns incorrect tenant-scoped data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is also a valid stored value. `loadAll` consequently returns an apparently successful array containing empty strings instead of reporting missing data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing map entry previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty value. The exported API therefore forces callers, including `loadAll`, to treat failed reads as valid data.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw at src/store.ts:4; it now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a stored empty value. loadAll consequently returns partial-looking data instead of reporting the missing entry.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config shape for retry
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers passing the previous public shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because both `retries` and `timeout` are required. JavaScript callers instead produce `deadline = NaN` when `timeout` is absent, so the deadline guard never stops retries and their configured timeout is ignored.

findings.title: Make retryBackground execute outside the caller stack
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background execution, but the implementation directly invokes `fn()` synchronously. A slow callback blocks the caller exactly as retry does; this is also a duplicate retry loop rather than a distinct background behavior.

findings.title: Expose failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: If every callback attempt throws, the catch discards each error and the exported function returns normal void, indistinguishable from a successful callback. Callers therefore cannot avoid treating an exhausted retry operation as successful.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and retry still accepts it, but callers using the previous documented shape ({ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }) now fail type checking because timeoutMs was removed and both retries and timeout are required.

findings.title: Return or report failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: Exceptions from fn are discarded, and retryBackground returns void both after success and after every attempt fails or the deadline expires. Its public callers therefore cannot distinguish a completed operation from a failed one.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers passing the previously required `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` config no longer compile. Untyped/JavaScript consumers instead pass `undefined` for `timeout`, making `Date.now() + undefined` become `NaN`; the timeout guard never fires and retries can exceed their former timeout.

findings.title: Expose terminal retry failure to retryBackground callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception is discarded and final exhaustion falls through a `void` return, which is indistinguishable from success. As an exported API, this forces all consumers to treat failed background work as successfully submitted or completed.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number, but number has no length property. TypeScript rejects this access, and a JavaScript consumer passing value={42} receives "len=undefined" rather than a meaningful label.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported prop now permits number, but the implementation still evaluates value.length. Numbers have no length property, so TypeScript rejects the component and numeric callers cannot use the newly advertised contract.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now permits `number`, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript reports an error for this expression, preventing the project from type-checking.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for patch output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` captures the complete `git diff mergeBase headSha` output at line 140. Omitting `maxBuffer` drops the prior 64 MiB limit to Node's 1 MiB default; a larger PR causes `spawnSync` to terminate the diff command, `git()` throws, and the review is posted as failed before analysis runs.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `runGithub` captures the complete `git diff` output at line 140. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default; a PR whose textual patch exceeds that limit returns a non-zero/error result, so line 38 throws and the review posts a failed check instead of reviewing the PR. The prior 64 MiB limit explicitly supported this path.

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync to Node's 1 MiB default. The patch is obtained through this helper at line 140, so a PR diff exceeding 1 MiB now causes spawnSync to fail and the review action posts a failed check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` defaults its sandbox policy to active configuration. A developer configuration can select `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`; because this process runs the model with `cwd` set to `opts.repoPath`, a review prompt can then modify or delete files in the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for Codex reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The spawned Codex process runs with cwd set to opts.repoPath. Removing `-s read-only` drops the only explicit filesystem restriction, so a review prompt or repository-supplied prompt injection can cause Codex to write, delete, or otherwise alter the repository under review.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates sandbox selection to the installed Codex default/profile. This process runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so a writable configured sandbox can let a prompt-driven review invocation alter the repository it is meant to inspect, including its review evidence. The previous invocation prevented that.

findings.title: Diff against the configured PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD (for example, a pull_request workflow checkout at GitHub's synthetic merge commit), the bundle declares headSha as PR_HEAD_SHA but generates patch and changedFiles against HEAD. The review can therefore analyze and comment on merge-commit changes while postReview/postCheck attach its result to PR_HEAD_SHA.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge base, not the current base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and the PR head branched earlier, baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD. `git diff baseSha HEAD` and the matching name-only query then include base-only commits as reverse changes, so Needlefish reviews files and content the PR author did not change. The prior code correctly derived the common merge base before constructing both inputs.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before generating the PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA can name the current base-branch tip rather than the PR's branch point. For a PR branch created before later base commits, `git diff PR_BASE_SHA HEAD` includes those base-only commits as deletions/changes, so the review bundle and inline-comment path set contain files the PR did not change.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt data during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement. Bundle JSON, candidate findings, or the raw patch can legitimately contain those sequences; for example `$&` is replaced with the matched placeholder rather than retained literally. This corrupts the prompt passed to either Codex review stage and can produce malformed or misleading reviews.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during placeholder replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace with a string replacement expands `$&`, `$`` and `$'`. Bundle JSON and bundle.patch contain arbitrary repository content, so a patch literal such as `$&` is changed into `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{PATCH}}` rather than passed to Codex verbatim; `$`` or `$'` additionally inject surrounding prompt text. Candidate findings can likewise contain these sequences at line 32. This makes the reviewer inspect a corrupted diff or critic input.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences when injecting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement specially: a diff containing `$&` is inserted as the matched placeholder (`{{PATCH}}`) instead of the literal source text; `$`` and `$'` inject the prompt prefix/suffix. Since bundle.patch is raw reviewed source, valid patches containing these JavaScript replacement tokens are silently altered before both the review and critic calls, which can hide or distort findings.

findings.title: Preserve the analyzed commit in the fallback review
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review request fails and a new commit is pushed before this fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's most recent commit. The body and verdict were computed from headSha, so a REQUEST_CHANGES review can block the newer commit even if it fixed the reported issue.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON request fails (for example, because an inline comment is no longer valid), this retry omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If a commit is pushed between collecting headSha and the retry, Needlefish submits findings computed for headSha as a review of the newer commit, potentially requesting changes on code it did not inspect.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit in the fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial request fails (for example, because an inline comment is invalid), this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run computed its result against headSha earlier. If the PR advances during review, Needlefish posts its verdict against unreviewed code.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid required finding data that previously raised a malformed-output error is now returned as a seemingly valid Finding (for example, invalid severity becomes P1 and missing file/lines become ""/0). Callers of this exported normalizer can no longer distinguish invalid review output from a real finding.

findings.title: Keep the strict option for existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported optional strict parameter breaks TypeScript consumers that call normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript consumers no longer get the documented permissive behavior of dropping malformed findings; they instead receive the fabricated records created at lines 98-109.

findings.title: Reject findings missing required location fields
findings.whyItBreaks: An incomplete finding such as {} is now returned as a Finding with file="" and lineStart/lineEnd=0. These values violate the previously enforced finding schema, so consumers that trust Finding records cannot locate or annotate the reported code.

findings.title: Preserve the strict normalization option
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported and previously accepted strict=false to discard malformed individual findings. Removing the parameter breaks typed callers at compile time; at runtime, an existing extra false argument is ignored and malformed findings become default-filled Finding records instead of being omitted.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid model output that previously raised an error now becomes a real-looking Finding (for example, an invalid severity becomes P1 while missing file and line fields become "" and 0). normalizeReview then returns these unusable findings to its public callers, which cannot distinguish malformed output from a valid review.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the public second parameter breaks TypeScript consumers that call normalizeReview(raw, false). It also removes the documented-by-behavior non-strict mode that previously discarded malformed individual findings instead of failing the whole review.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any actions/checkout step. `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` therefore has no checked-out repository or `GH_REPO` context from which to infer the target repository. The command fails instead of producing head/base SHAs, breaking the documented manual PR review path.

findings.title: Keep explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, this step runs before actions/checkout, so gh has no checked-out repository remote from which to infer a repository. Without -R "$REPO" (or GH_REPO), gh pr view cannot reliably resolve PR_NUM; on a clean runner the manual review fails before checkout, and a stale self-hosted workspace could target the wrong repository.

findings.title: Restore the explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this step runs before any checkout. `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` therefore has no repository to infer from the working directory, so resolving head/base fails and the checkout/review never starts.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid top-level fields now become empty strings/arrays instead of raising the prior malformed-output error. Since normalizeReview is exported, callers cannot distinguish an invalid reviewer response from a legitimate review with no findings, no checks, and no residual risks.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or an object missing findings, checked, or residual_risks previously threw a malformed-review error. They now return a valid-looking RawReview with empty arrays and an empty summary, so consumers cannot distinguish failed/invalid review generation from a review that found nothing.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors instead of emitting an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously rejected for missing required review fields now become a syntactically valid RawReview with an empty summary and no findings, checks, or blocking risks. Because normalizeReview is exported, callers cannot distinguish malformed model output from a genuine empty review and may treat an invalid review as a clean result.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for manual review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this checks out github.ref (the branch selected to run the workflow), not the required pr_number's head. The same event also leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty at lines 45-46 and fetches main rather than the target PR's base branch. Previously the workflow resolved all three refs with `gh pr view`, so manually triggering a review can now run against unrelated source and lacks the requested PR's revision metadata.

findings.title: Resolve workflow-dispatch PR refs before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this falls back to github.ref rather than the PR selected by inputs.pr_number. The self-review workflow then installs and runs the default/dispatch branch’s Needlefish code instead of the PR head; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty on lines 45-46. Previously the Resolve PR refs step queried the selected PR and supplied its exact head and base.

findings.title: Resolve requested PR refs for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. A run launched from main with pr_number for a PR whose head is another branch therefore checks out github.ref (main), ignoring the requested PR number. The workflow's documented self-review contract requires the PR checkout's own source to be the tool, so manual reviews can execute stale/wrong tool and configuration code.

findings.title: Restore the git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. runLocal obtains the entire patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at lines 98-100; a diff exceeding 1 MiB now causes spawnSync to fail and git() throws before review() is called. The previous implementation supported patches up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Keep a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the complete patch with `git diff` before calling the reviewer. Omitting `maxBuffer` restores `spawnSync`'s 1 MiB default, so a larger diff terminates with a buffer error and the review aborts instead of producing a result. The prior 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for patch output
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the complete patch with `git diff` at line 100. With no `maxBuffer`, spawnSync uses Node’s 1 MiB default; a larger diff fails with ENOBUFS, so the local reviewer aborts before submitting the review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these ordinary large PRs.

findings.title: Report review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a neutral required status check as successful. When review() or reporting fails, this now publishes a neutral Needlefish check even though the summary says the PR did not pass, so a branch requiring Needlefish can still be merged.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: A thrown review/posting error previously produced a failure conclusion, but now produces neutral. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required status, so a required Needlefish check can allow merging even though the review did not complete.

findings.title: Bind PR diff retrieval to the requested repository
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub accepts cwd and identifies its target with GITHUB_REPOSITORY, but gh pr diff resolves its repository from the process working directory unless --repo is supplied. When cwd differs from process.cwd, metadata and git operations target the requested repository while patch retrieval targets another repository (or fails), producing an incorrect review bundle.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(), posting, or rendering throws, the dedicated "Needlefish" check now receives conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a protected branch requiring this check can merge despite the review never completing.

findings.title: Restore a trusted checkout for the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The only checkout now resolves to the PR head (lines 43-47), so this invokes a PR-controlled src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN, whose workflow permissions include pull-requests: write and checks: write. An internal PR can alter the reviewer to suppress findings or use the token/runner context; the removed separate checkout explicitly prevented this.

findings.title: Keep the tool checkout or add the local tool files
findings.whyItBreaks: The reviewed head tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, src/cli.ts, or node_modules. pnpm install --frozen-lockfile therefore cannot install in the checkout, and the review command at line 59 cannot exist even if installation were skipped.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR-head checkout contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, lockfile, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` therefore cannot install a project, and the review command cannot start, so every review workflow fails.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer code outside the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head at lines 43-47, then installs and executes its package and `src/cli.ts`. A same-repository PR can alter either the install lifecycle or reviewer implementation to suppress findings or forge review/check output while `GH_TOKEN` is present and the job has `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` permissions. This removes the previous trusted-main boundary and lets a PR control its own approval mechanism.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the installed reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: At the head SHA, the repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json. It has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules setup, or src/cli.ts, so pnpm install fails before the review command can run.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external data and passes each finding to this exported normalizer. A valid severity such as " p2 " or "p2" previously became "P2"; it now fails the exact-membership check and is silently classified as "P3", changing the reported priority.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` accepts untyped review JSON and delegates each finding here. A previously accepted value such as `" p1 "` or `"p0"` now fails the exact-membership check and is returned as `P3`, silently lowering the finding's severity instead of preserving its intended classification.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external review JSON and passes each finding to this function. A severity such as "p0" or " P1 ", which previously normalized to P0/P1, now fails the exact-match check and is silently reclassified as P3. This can downgrade a high-severity review finding.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex child process
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. A GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN present in the runner becomes available to the prompted Codex subprocess, which can read and use that credential despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit env allowlist/scrubbing makes spawnSync inherit GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked Codex process can read its environment despite the read-only filesystem sandbox, so a prompt-influenced agent run can disclose credentials through its output or use them for GitHub API access.

findings.title: Continue stripping GitHub credentials before invoking Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. This restores GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN to the Codex child process, allowing prompt- or repository-influenced Codex activity to use the caller's GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running on the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The pull_request workflow now accepts fork PRs, checks out the attacker-controlled head SHA, then runs pnpm install and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can alter the lockfile, install inputs, or reviewed source to execute arbitrary commands in that runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for self-hosted execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now enter this job, which checks out the fork-controlled head at line 23 and executes its src/cli.ts at line 34 on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can modify that entrypoint or its imports to execute arbitrary code and compromise the runner or its accessible credentials/state.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach this job, which checks out the contributor-controlled head SHA and executes both pnpm install and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can modify that code to run arbitrary commands in the runner environment and access any runner-local credentials or state.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner shutdown delays
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting either NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS to "0" produced an immediate next shutdown step. This condition now rejects 0 and silently substitutes 5000 ms or 2000 ms, respectively, so configured immediate termination can be delayed by seconds.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, both NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were accepted and passed to their setTimeout calls, allowing immediate SIGKILL escalation and immediate give-up after it. This change silently substitutes 5000 ms and 2000 ms respectively, so existing deployments configured for no delay now wait up to seven additional seconds after a runner timeout.

findings.title: Preserve explicit zero-duration overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were accepted, allowing immediate SIGKILL escalation and immediate completion after SIGKILL. This change maps both explicit values to 5000ms and 2000ms respectively, altering established environment configuration behavior on upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep pass can return residual_risks that require a blocked verdict, but this code replaces them with an empty array before invoking the critic and deriving the final verdict. The prior implementation accumulated these risks, so an incomplete large review can now be reported as unblocked.

findings.title: Return a blocked result when one deep pass fails
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview/extractJson/runCodex failures from any one hotspot now reject reviewLarge immediately. Previously the failure was represented as a blocking residual risk and the other hotspots still completed, so a transient malformed or failed deep review now makes every large review fail without a review result.

findings.title: Deep-review changed files omitted from selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only the first six mapped hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means any changed file not included in those selected hotspots is never sent to deep review, allowing defects in those files to be silently missed.

findings.title: Restore deep-review coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapper-selected hotspots are deep-reviewed. Removing the tail hotspot means any changed file omitted by the mapper, or assigned to a hotspot beyond that cap, receives no deep review. The critic receives only the merged findings and a diff stat, so it has no file contents from which to recover defects in skipped files.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep-review residual risks, including blocks=true signals for incomplete evidence, are no longer accumulated and the critic is explicitly given residual_risks: []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a complete deep review from one that reported an unresolved blocking risk, and deriveVerdict can return a non-blocked verdict for an incompletely reviewed PR.

findings.title: Review every changed file in large patches
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapper-selected hotspots are reviewed. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot leaves changed files omitted by the mapper, or hotspots beyond MAX_HOTSPOTS, completely unreviewed; the critic receives no indication of that gap and can approve a large PR containing an unchecked defect.

findings.title: Forward residual risks from successful deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can report a blocking residual risk even when it completes successfully, but this assignment replaces all of those signals with an empty array before the critic sees them. The final result can therefore present a verdict without the unresolved evidence that should block it.

score.error: malformed critic output: residual risk was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Preserve focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When a patch exceeds the large-review threshold, review() routes to reviewLarge(), which no longer includes bundle.focus in either the mapping input or each deep-review prompt. A caller requesting a focused review therefore gets an unfocused large review, while small reviews still serialize the full Bundle including focus.

findings.title: Preserve the focus option for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep-review prompt no longer substitutes bundle.focus. A focused review is therefore honored by reviewSmall (which serializes the full Bundle) but ignored whenever isLarge routes the same request through reviewLarge, causing large PRs to review unrelated areas instead of the requested scope.

findings.title: Normalize rounding carry into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remaining seconds round to 60, the formatter does not carry that second into minutes. For example, 599500ms renders as `9m 60s` (and 59500ms as `60s`) rather than the normalized `10m 0s` / `1m 0s` shown in review statistics.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remaining seconds round to 60, such as 119500ms, this renders `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. Both per-call and total durations are emitted in the public Markdown output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, rendering "1m 60s". The prior behavior rounded the whole duration and rendered "2m 0s"; stats and total durations near each minute boundary are now displayed incorrectly.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger promises a positive integer, but the changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0. Public callers can rely on the name/error contract when validating values such as timeouts or attempt counts.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0, while both its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. External callers can rely on this validator to reject zero for values such as retry attempts or durations and instead receive an invalid zero value.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger` and its error text promise a positive integer, but the changed `< 0` guard returns `0` successfully. External callers can now accept zero for values whose contract requires a strictly positive value.
